newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: FOCUS-SLOVAKIA SOLID BUT MUST SPEED UP REFORM - OECD.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-SLOVAKIA SOLID BUT MUST SPEED UP REFORM - OECD.

text.p: Slovakia's economic
development since independence in 1993 exceeded negative
forecasts but more reform is needed, the Organisation for
Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said on Monday.
In its first full survey devoted to Slovakia, the club of
the world's richest countries forecast Slovak real gross
domestic product (GDP) to grow at around six percent in 1996,
slowing slightly to five percent growth in 1997.
It said that the annual inflation rate, which has fallen
from double-digits in the past year, would remain stuck through
1997 at about six percent.
The OECD said Slovakia had managed to stabilise the economy
and had the lowest inflation among post-Communist states.
But there were several areas of concern in the process of
economic restructuring, including privatisation by direct sales
which resulted in concentrated ownership and did not guarantee
better business performance.
"In general, there is need for greater transparency and
accountability (in privatisation)...so that selection criteria
and decisions can be fully assesed," it said.
It also called on the government to further reduce its
influence in strategic companies to enable more competition.
State influence was still predominant in key industrial
sectors despite the fact that the private sector accounts
roughly for about two-thirds of the Slovakia's GDP, it said.
Slovakia has appeared hesitant to accept and fully utilise
market-based mechanisms in pricing and resource allocation.
There has also been some hesitancy in accepting foreign
capital and participation in the economy, the survey added.
"There is no economic justification for such tendencies
continuing in a still under-capitalised economy," it said.
"With growth prospects so heavily dependent on export
performance, Slovakia needs to be open to all possible forms of
external economic interactions."
The OECD warned that the current competetive advantages of
some Slovak exports were not indefinite and that the country
needed to adapt to conditions of increased competition.
The official Slovak Statistical Bureau (SUSR) said last
week that Slovakia's real GDP rose 7.1 percent year-on-year in
the first half of this year.
But according to SUSR's latest forecast, full-year 1996
real GDP is expected to grow by 6.4 to 7.0 percent, compared to
a previous projection of 7.1 percent growth.
The bureau attributed the revision to falling export demand
and the central bank's tighter monetary policy.
